name: The Sol Route
tagline: 8 riddles from the Puerta del Sol to the Templo de Debod

stops.riddle: Every road in Spain begins at my feet.
stops.whereHint: Puerta del Sol, in front of the building with the clock.
stops.look: Find the plaque in the pavement
stops.question: What distance is written on the plaque?

lesson.title: Kilómetro Cero

image.alt: The Puerta del Sol, with the old Royal Post Office and its clock tower

lesson.subtitle: The point every main road in Spain is measured from
lesson.recap: Where Spain’s main roads are measured from

story.text: The Puerta del Sol was once one of the gates of Madrid’s town walls. Its name means “Gate of the Sun”.
In the 18th century Spain built its six national roads out from Madrid, starting where the royal mail riders set off: right on this square.
The building behind the plaque was the Royal Post Office. Every New Year’s Eve, Spain watches its clock on TV and eats one grape at each of the 12 chimes.

timeline.text: Spain’s six national roads are built out from Madrid
The New Year chimes are first broadcast on national TV
The old post office becomes the seat of Madrid’s regional government

context.title: A country shaped like a wheel
context.text: Spain’s main road network is radial: like the spokes of a wheel, the big national roads run from Madrid out to the coasts and borders. That is why distances on road signs all over Spain count from this plaque.

lookCloser.title: The plaque.
lookCloser.text: Read the words around the “0”. It sits in the pavement in front of the old post office door.

lookCloser.title: The clock tower.
lookCloser.text: Look up: this is the clock all of Spain counts down with on New Year’s Eve.

lesson.think: Why would a country measure all its roads from its capital, and not from its biggest port or its geographic centre?

check.question: What do people in Spain eat at the 12 New Year chimes?

stops.riddle: Find the beast that eats from the tree.
stops.whereHint: A bronze statue on the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s favourite meeting point.
stops.question: Which tree is the bear reaching into?
stops.hint: Its Spanish name is part of the statue’s name.

lesson.title: El Oso y el Madroño

image.alt: The bronze bear reaching into the strawberry tree, with the clock tower behind it

lesson.subtitle: Madrid’s coat of arms, cast in bronze
lesson.recap: Madrid’s symbol, on this square since 1967

numbers.label: symbols: a bear and a tree

story.text: A bear reaching into a strawberry tree has stood for Madrid on its coat of arms for centuries.
This statue turned the coat of arms into something you can meet beside. It was unveiled in 1967 on the east side of the square, between Calle de Alcalá and Carrera de San Jerónimo.
It has been moved several times as the square was redesigned, but people in Madrid still say “quedamos en el oso”: meet you at the bear.

timeline.text: The statue is unveiled in the Puerta del Sol
Moved several times as the square is remodelled

context.title: What is a coat of arms?
context.text: Cities, like noble families, used a coat of arms as their badge. Madrid’s shows the bear and the madroño under a crown, with seven stars around them.

lookCloser.title: The fruit.
lookCloser.text: Look for the small round berries on the tree. Madroño fruit is red when ripe.

lookCloser.title: The crowd.
lookCloser.text: Count how many people are waiting for someone here right now.

lesson.think: If your town had a coat of arms, which animal or plant would you put on it, and why?

stops.riddle: A king on horseback guards the great square.
stops.whereHint: The big arcaded square just west of Sol.
stops.look: Read the base of the statue
stops.question: Who rides the horse?
stops.hint: He was the son of the king who made Madrid the capital.

lesson.title: Plaza Mayor

image.alt: The Plaza Mayor, with the statue of Felipe III in front of the painted Casa de la Panadería

lesson.subtitle: The great square of Habsburg Madrid, and the city’s stage for 400 years

story.text: this was the Plaza del Arrabal: an open market just outside the old town walls.
King Felipe II moved his court here in 1561 and the town grew fast. It needed a grand main square, and his son Felipe III had the architect Juan Gómez de Mora finish it in 1619.
Markets, bullfights, royal celebrations and even the public trials of the Inquisition took place here. Fire swept through the square several times, and each time it was rebuilt.

timeline.text: Felipe II makes Madrid the capital of Spain
The bronze statue of Felipe III is cast
Juan Gómez de Mora finishes the square
The first great fire; the square is rebuilt
The statue is moved here from the Casa de Campo

context.title: Madrid de los Austrias
context.text: The Habsburgs, called “los Austrias” in Spain, ruled from 1516 to 1700. The old streets around this square, from Sol to the palace, still carry their name. Most of today’s route is in their Madrid.

lookCloser.title: The bronze king.
lookCloser.text: Cast in 1616 by Giambologna and Pietro Tacca. It stood in the Casa de Campo park until 1848.

lookCloser.title: The painted façade.
lookCloser.text: The Casa de la Panadería is named after the bakery that once stood on its site.

lookCloser.title: The ten arches.
lookCloser.text: Can you find the one with steep steps? That’s where you’re heading next.

lesson.think: Why would a king want a huge, closed square right in the middle of his new capital?

check.question: In which year did Madrid become the capital?

stops.riddle: Go down the steep steps. The street below remembers an old trade.
stops.whereHint: The arch in the south-west corner of the Plaza Mayor.
stops.look: Read the name of the arch
stops.question: Who used to work on the street below?

lesson.title: Arco de Cuchilleros

image.alt: The Arco de Cuchilleros: a stone arch with steps, seen from the street below

lesson.subtitle: The steep way down to old Madrid’s taverns
lesson.recap: Steps down to Botín, open since 1725

story.text: The Plaza Mayor sits higher than the streets below it, so this corner exit is a steep stairway through an arch.
The arch takes its name from the street below, Calle de Cuchilleros, the street of the cutlers: the knife makers.
At the bottom is Botín, founded in 1725 and listed by Guinness World Records as the oldest restaurant in the world. Ernest Hemingway set the final scene of The Sun Also Rises there.

timeline.text: Botín opens at the foot of the steps
Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises is published

context.title: Streets named after trades
context.text: Old Madrid named many streets after the craftspeople who worked there. Keep an eye out on the route for other trade names, like Calle de Bordadores, the street of the embroiderers.

lookCloser.title: The steps.
lookCloser.text: Count them on your way down. How steep is the slope from the square?

lookCloser.title: Botín’s sign.
lookCloser.text: Find the restaurant at the bottom and the year on its front.

lesson.think: Why do you think the oldest taverns grew up right next to the main square?

check.question: Which writer set a famous scene at Botín?

stops.riddle: Where the city bought its fish and fruit, under a roof of iron.
stops.whereHint: A glass market hall just west of the Plaza Mayor.
stops.look: Look at how the market is built
stops.question: What holds up the glass walls?

lesson.title: Mercado de San Miguel

image.alt: The Mercado de San Miguel, an iron and glass market hall

lesson.subtitle: An iron market hall from 1916, reborn as a food hall

story.text: The market takes its name from the church of San Miguel that once stood on this spot.
Architect Alfonso Dubé y Díez gave it an iron frame inspired by Les Halles in Paris. It opened on 13 May 1916.
After years of decline it was restored and reopened in 2009 as a gourmet food market, one of the first of its kind in Spain.

timeline.text: Work on the iron market begins
The market opens on 13 May
It reopens as a gourmet food market

context.title: The age of iron
context.text: Around 1900, iron and glass let architects build big, bright spaces quickly. Train stations, greenhouses and market halls like this one went up all over Europe.

lookCloser.title: The iron columns.
lookCloser.text: Look up and follow how they carry the roof.

lookCloser.title: The glass walls.
lookCloser.text: They were fitted around the original iron frame in the restoration.

lesson.think: When an old local market becomes a place for visitors, who gains and who loses?

check.question: Which city’s market inspired its design?

stops.riddle: An admiral stands where the city was once governed.
stops.whereHint: A small square on Calle Mayor, by the old town hall.
stops.look: Read the name on the pedestal
stops.question: Which admiral is honoured by the statue?

lesson.title: Plaza de la Villa

image.alt: The Plaza de la Villa, with the old town hall and the admiral’s statue

lesson.subtitle: Where Madrid was governed for centuries

story.text: Around you stand the Torre de los Lujanes from the 15th century, the Casa de Cisneros from 1537, and the Casa de la Villa, Madrid’s old town hall.
The town hall was designed by Juan Gómez de Mora, the architect of the Plaza Mayor, and begun in the 1640s. Madrid’s city council met here until 2007.
In the middle stands Álvaro de Bazán, a commander of the 16th-century Spanish navy who fought at the battle of Lepanto in 1571. Mariano Benlliure’s bronze was unveiled in 1891.

timeline.text: The Torre de los Lujanes is built
The Casa de Cisneros is built
Work begins on the town hall
The statue of Álvaro de Bazán is unveiled
The city council moves out

context.title: Three styles, side by side
context.text: The tower is Mudéjar: Christian building with Islamic-style brickwork. The Casa de Cisneros is Plateresque, carved as finely as silverwork. The town hall is Baroque. Spot the difference as you turn around.

lookCloser.title: The covered bridge.
lookCloser.text: An arch links the town hall to the Casa de Cisneros next door.

lookCloser.title: The admiral’s armour.
lookCloser.text: He is shown in half armour. Look at the details on his chest plate.

lesson.think: Why might a city move its town hall out of its oldest square?

check.question: Until when did the city council meet here?

stops.riddle: The king’s house looks at the queen of heaven.
stops.whereHint: The big square between the Royal Palace and the cathedral.
stops.look: Stand with your back to the palace
stops.question: Which church faces the Royal Palace?

lesson.title: Royal Palace

image.alt: Aerial view of the Royal Palace, with the Almudena Cathedral just behind it

lesson.subtitle: A palace built on the ashes of a fortress
lesson.recap: Begun in 1738 after the Alcázar burned

story.text: Madrid began here as a Muslim fortress on the hill above the river Manzanares. It later became the royal Alcázar.

On Christmas Eve 1734 the Alcázar caught fire and burned for days. King Felipe V ordered a new palace of stone and brick. Filippo Juvarra designed it; after his death Giovanni Battista Sacchetti adapted the plan, and the first stone was laid in 1738.
With around 3,000 rooms it is the official residence of the King of Spain, used today for state ceremonies. Across the square, the Almudena Cathedral was consecrated in 1993 by Pope John Paul II.

timeline.text: A Muslim fortress is built on this hill
The Alcázar burns on Christmas Eve
The first stone of the new palace is laid
The Almudena Cathedral is consecrated

context.title: Madrid’s Muslim beginnings
context.text: Madrid started as Mayrit, a fortress built in the 9th century by the emirs of Córdoba to watch over this hill. The Alcázar and then the palace grew on the same spot.

lookCloser.title: The view west.
lookCloser.text: Walk to the railings: the hill drops towards the river and the Casa de Campo park.

lookCloser.title: Palace vs cathedral.
lookCloser.text: Stand between them. The palace took about 25 years to build; the cathedral more than a century.

lesson.think: Why build the new palace exactly where the old one burned, instead of somewhere new?

check.question: When did the old Alcázar burn?

stops.riddle: Follow the sun to the temple that crossed the sea.
stops.whereHint: A park on the hill north of the palace.
stops.question: Which country gave this temple to Spain?

lesson.title: Templo de Debod

image.alt: The Templo de Debod and its two stone gateways, in a Madrid park

lesson.subtitle: A 2,200-year-old Egyptian temple in a Madrid park

story.text: The temple was built in the 2nd century BC near Aswan, in Nubia in southern Egypt, and dedicated to the gods Amun and Isis.
When the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s, the rising Nile threatened Nubia’s temples. Spain helped save them, including Abu Simbel, and in 1968 Egypt gave Debod to Spain as thanks.
It was shipped in pieces and rebuilt here, on the site of the old Cuartel de la Montaña barracks, and opened in 1972. Today it is one of the best places in Madrid to watch the sunset.

timeline.text: The temple is built near Aswan
The Aswan High Dam threatens Nubia’s temples
Egypt gives the temple to Spain
It opens to the public in Madrid

context.title: Saving the Nubian monuments
context.text: In the 1960s UNESCO led an international campaign to move Nubia’s temples before the waters rose. Several countries that helped received a temple as thanks: New York, Leiden and Turin each have one too.

lookCloser.title: The gateways.
lookCloser.text: Walk through the two stone gateways that stand in front of the temple.

lookCloser.title: The carvings.
lookCloser.text: Look for hieroglyphs on the stone, more than 2,000 years old.

lesson.think: Is it better to move a monument far away to save it, or to leave it where it was built?

check.question: Why did Egypt give Spain this temple?
options: To thank Spain for helping save Nubian temples
check.answer: To thank Spain for helping save Nubian temples
